For what reason? Because..."
The thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) and the master (*ācārya*) are non-dual; this is an indivisible unity.
To speak briefly, O son of noble family: as many Buddhas as there are in the world-systems of the ten directions...
And all those bodhisattvas, who remain, stay, and maintain themselves, come three times a day,
worship that master with all the offerings to the Tathāgatas, and then return once more to their respective buddha-fields, uttering these words of the vajra-syllables: "He is our father."
She is the mother of all Tathāgatas, our teacher of all Tathāgatas.
Son of good family, it is just as if there were as many Blessed Buddhas as there are dwelling in the ten directions; of those Blessed Buddhas, up to...

The mass of merit born from the vajras of body, speech, and mind—that mass of merit is even more distinguished when it enters into the pores of the very skin of the master. Why is that? Noble son, the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) is the essence of all the gnoses of the Buddhas, the source of their arising, and so forth.
"It is the source of the knowledge of the omniscient one.
Then, indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya, being afraid and with a terrified mind, became silent. [k: tormented]
Then indeed, the Tathāgata Akṣobhya, the Tathāgata Ratnaketu, the Tathāgata Amitāyus, the Tathāgata Amoghasiddhi,
and the Tathāgata Vairocana, having entered the samādhi named *Sarvadharmasiddhisamayālambanavajra*, addressed all these bodhisattvas.

"Listen, O Blessed Ones, all you Bodhisattvas! Even those Blessed Buddhas in the ten directions, who have arisen from the vajra-wisdom of the three times—they too all come to honor and pay homage to the Master who has received initiation into the Guhyasamāja. For what reason? Because..."
The Teacher of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and of all Tathāgatas, is that very Blessed One Mahāvajradhara, the Sovereign of the Wisdom of all Buddhas. (pdf 94, 139)

Then all those great bodhisattvas said this to all the tathāgatas: "Blessed Ones, where do the accomplishments of the body, speech, and mind of all tathāgatas reside, and from where have they arisen? All the tathāgatas replied: "In the secret of the three bodies."

The body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas abide within the vajra of the body, speech, and mind of the Vajrācārya. The Mahābodhisattvas asked: "Where does the secret vajra of body, speech, and mind abide? All the Tathāgatas replied: "It abides in space. The Mahābodhisattvas asked: "Where does space abide?"
All the Tathāgatas replied, "Nowhere. Then those great Bodhisattvas, having attained a state of wonder and amazement, remained silent.
Then the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Vajrapāṇi—

Rising from the samādhi of the secret vajra of the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas— [Vajradhara, as added in k and d]— he addressed all the Tathāgatas and all the Bodhisattvas: "Listen, O Blessed Ones, all Tathāgatas and all Bodhisattvas!"
The Great Maṇḍala named the Vajra Source of All Tathāgatas and Bodhisattvas.
Then, all the Tathāgatas and Bodhisattvas, with palms joined in reverence, spoke thus to the Blessed One, the Holder of the Vajra: "May the Blessed One teach! May the Sugata teach the great maṇḍala!"
One should contemplate a most beautiful square situated in the center of the space-element;
through the yoga of the Buddha-maṇḍala, one should impel the meditation-vajra.
Through the meditation on the vajra-maṇḍala, the wise one should always perform the seat for all the wheel-bearers according to that very same ritual procedure.
Having meditated upon the Ācārya in one’s heart, one should commence the consecration;
one should contemplate the space-element as completely filled with all the Buddhas.
One should cause all [beings] to fall [into the state of enlightenment] according to the rule by means of the three stages of consecration;
through this, one attains the awakening that seeks the welfare of all sentient beings.
Body, speech, and mind are accomplished, the great wonder of all siddhis.
The Meditation Maṇḍala named the Samaya-Wheel of All Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

Then indeed, Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of all Tathāgatas, once again brought forth from the vajras of his own body, speech, and mind the secret of body, speech, and mind called the "Vajrayoga of All Tathāgatas" (or the "Vajra of Yoga").
HŪṂ HRĪḤ KHAṂ.
One should contemplate the mandala of bone, flesh, and so forth situated in the center of the space-element;
within the heart of the body, speech, and mind of the three kāyas, one should visualize Vajrasattva.
One should visualize him as fierce, deformed, and enraged, with a luster like that of a blue lotus; he has four arms and, according to the ritual injunction, holds a skull in his hand.
The practitioner should visualize his own tongue as being illuminated by five-colored rays of light;
through the application of meditation and mantra, this is the supreme method for summoning blood.
The trident, the vajra-samaya, and the most formidable supreme stake—one should personally crush even the body of a Buddha by means of the vajra-yoga. Thus it is said.

Then Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of all Tathāgatas, once again, for the sake of the ritual activity of the Vajra-food samaya, emitted [this teaching] from the vajras of his own body, speech, and mind: "Whether it be food or drink, whatever the practitioner should consume,"
One should fashion it according to the prescribed rule by means of feces, urine, and flesh.

(From PDF 95, p. 141) Then Vajrapāṇi, the lord of all Tathāgatas, once again emitted from his own body, speech, and mind-vajras the supreme assembly of the body, speech, and mind-vajras of all Tathāgatas.
One should also perform worship with the five supreme offerings;
for this is the samaya of all Vajras, which is difficult to transgress.
Then Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of all Tathāgatas, once again emitted from the vajras of his own body, speech, and mind the secret of the worship of the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas:
"By means of the application of the two organs and by taking up one's own semen and so forth."
One should worship them all according to the prescribed rite, and one shall attain the enlightenment of a Buddha.
Then Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of all Tathāgatas, once again emitted from the vajras of his own body, speech, and mind the vow of the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas—
the mother of the infinite realm of sentient beings, who upholds the samaya.
Through the three-vajra commitments regarding the body, this is the most wonderful vow.
Then Vajrapāṇi, the sovereign of all Tathāgatas, once again emitted from the vajras of his own body, speech, and mind the Vajra of the Samvara of all practitioners,
which is the enjoyment of body, speech, and mind.
Born from the vajra of the abode of the three secrets, I shall accomplish this auspicious goal; there is no doubt whatsoever in this matter.
Then Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of all Tathāgatas, once again issued forth from the vajras of his own body, speech, and mind the commitment (*samvara*) of the Vajrasattva of all practitioners.
Having stepped forward a distance of one *vitasti*, one should visualize a mandala upon the head;
having meditated on the syllable *Oṃ* situated in its center, one effects the descent of the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*).
By means of this vajra-yoga, one becomes radiant in an instant;
the well-being of body, speech, and mind is attained—of this there is no doubt.
Then Vajrapāṇi, the lord of all Tathāgatas, [expounded] once again the secret of the body, speech, and mind of the holders of all maṇḍalas.
[The Mantra: He caused it to issue forth from the vajras of his own body, speech, and mind:
"One should not perform the rite of caityas, nor the recitation of books;
one should by no means construct a maṇḍala, nor perform the prostration to the supreme Three Vajras."
Then Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of all Tathāgatas, emitted from the vajras of his own body, speech, and mind the secret [mantra] for the removal, immobilization, and summoning of all poisons: *bhruṃ*.
Having placed it in the center of the wheel, one should meditate upon it as being yellowish in appearance, garlanded with a blaze of white rays and dense with yellow rays of light;
this seed-syllable is born from the secret, through the commitments of the rays of the three vajras.
Then Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of all Tathāgatas, emitted from the vajras of his own body, speech, and mind the mantra for the wheel of protection of body, speech, and mind, conjoined with the vajra:
*uṃ hūlū hūlū tiṣṭha tiṣṭha bandha bandha hana hana daha daha amṛte hūṃ phaṭ*.
Svāhā! (pdf 96, p.
143) On birch bark and other materials, one should draw the wheel established upon the karma-vajra.
Having placed the syllable *haṃ* in the middle of the letter *ha*, one should write it in the middle of the name.
One should always install [the deity] properly adorned with the syllables and words of the mantra;
for this is the source of the abode of the three secrets of all mantras.

Then Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of all Tathāgatas, emitted the Vajra-anjana formula from the vajras of his own body, speech, and mind: "At a crossroads, at a solitary tree, at a maternity home, or in a temple of Śiva."
One should always cast the substance of vajra-añjana there into the skull-cup.
Having prepared *mahātaila*, blood, excrement, lotus-fiber, and *arka*-cotton [as a wick], the wise one should cause *vajrāñjana* to fall at midnight on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight;
having consecrated it right there eight hundred times, threefold accomplishment occurs— thus said the Blessed One.
Samantabhadra. Then all the Blessed Tathāgatas spoke thus to Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of all Tathāgatas:
"Blessed One, with how many secret syllables are those Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas endowed who [practice] this?"
They will have faith in and cultivate the vajra of the conduct of all Tathāgatas and the secret samaya of all Tathāgatas.
Then Vajrapāṇi, the sovereign of all Tathāgatas—

He spoke thus to all those Tathāgatas: "O Blessed Ones, all Tathāgatas, those Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who shall have faith in and cultivate this Vajra of the Awakening Conduct of all Tathāgatas are endowed with the three secret syllables. All the Tathāgatas asked: "By which three? Vajradhara replied:
He said: namely, by means of these three—the body-vajra of all Tathāgatas, the speech-vajra of all Tathāgatas, and the mind-vajra of all Tathāgatas. (pdf 97, p. 144)
Then all those Tathāgatas, having prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One Vajrapāṇi, remained silent.
Then Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of all Tathāgatas, addressed those Tathāgatas and Bodhisattvas:
"In the past, O Blessed Ones, all Tathāgatas..."

Eons as numerous as the atoms in the Sumeru mountains of unspeakably unspeakable Buddha-fields have passed, yet from the time of the passing of the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Dīpaṅkara, until the time of the Great Sage Kāśyapa who had attained perfect enlightenment, this was not spoken. For what reason? Because they were incapable.
"O Blessed Ones, sentient beings are not fit to practice this matter of the great secret;

therefore, at that time and at that occasion, it was not spoken by me. However, O Blessed Ones, all Tathāgatas accomplish the awakening of a Buddha in this *Guhyasamāja* in a mere instant, a moment, or a brief duration."

That which Bodhisattvas do not attain as enlightenment even by striving and exerting themselves for many eons equal to the sands of the river Ganges— here, in this very life, a Bodhisattva who delights in the *Guhyasamāja* enters into the reckoning of being a Buddha among all the Tathāgatas.
Then those great bodhisattvas, having heard these syllables of the speech-vajra, wept aloud.

Then all those Tathāgatas spoke thus to those bodhisattvas: "O Blessed Great Bodhisattvas, do not weep, and do not give rise to the threefold suffering. Then those great bodhisattvas [spoke] to them...
All the Tathāgatas spoke thus: "O Blessed Ones, all you Tathāgatas, why do we not weep? Why do we not give rise to suffering? And for what reason? (pdf 97, p. 145)

"O Blessed Ones, you are incapable [of understanding] the three secret syllables; O Blessed Ones, you are incapable even of hearing their names. All the Tathāgatas said: "Noble sons, just as this word of common syllables has not been known or heard by you, so too has it not been known or heard by us, all the Tathāgatas."
Furthermore, O sons of good family, those secret syllables have not been attained nor fully awakened to by any of the Buddhas or Bodhisattvas.
Why is that? Because of the purity of the three secret syllables.
Then all those Bodhisattvas remained silent. Then...
The Blessed Ones, all the Tathāgatas, dwelt within the wombs of the Vajra Ladies of the body, speech, and mind of all the Tathāgatas.

Then that beloved of the minds of all the Tathāgatas, Māmakī, joyfully praised the Blessed One, the Sovereign of all Tathāgatas, Mahāvajradhara, with these supreme syllables of worship consisting of the delight of passion for the Vajra-holder:
[O Prajñāpāramitā: O Vajra-mind, Lord of the World, protect me, O essence of beings, with your delightful passion for the sake of the great purpose!
Desire me, O Father, supreme kinsman of beings; if you wish for my life, O Gentle Lord!

Then that Buddhalocanā, the beloved of the bodies of all Tathāgatas, praised the Blessed One, the Lord of all Tathāgatas, the Great Vajradhara, with these supreme syllables of worship for the delight of all vajra-desires, out of joy, gladness, and rapture.
O Vajra-body, you whose embrace is dear to many beings, who perceive the welfare of the ultimate meaning of awakening and the purpose of the Buddhas:
if you so desire, please gratify me with passion according to the passion-samaya.
O Mañjunātha, [this is] my life.

(From *pdf* 98, p. 146) Then that beloved consort of Lokeśvara, the Netrī residing in the body— [the Netrī of the Vajras of Body, Speech, and Mind]— [served] the Blessed One, the Lord of all Tathāgatas, Mahāvajradhara, with the pledges of the enjoyment of sensual pleasures.
He praised him.
O Vajravāc, you who are compassionate for the welfare of all and ever engaged in performing deeds for the sake of the world;
O Samantabhadra, grant me [the union of] passionate conduct, if you desire my life, O Mañjunātha!

Then she, the consort of the Vajra of the Pledge of the Body, Speech, and Mind of all Tathāgatas, praised the Blessed One, the Sovereign of all Tathāgatas, the Great Vajradhara, with this joy, gladness,
and delight of all Tathāgatas: "O Vajra-Body, supreme pledge, for the sake of great benefit..."
The ornament of the lineage of the Perfectly Awakened Ones, compassionate and impartial,
O Mañjunātha, if you desire my life, then accept me, a treasury of virtues who have become like a mine of many jewels.

Then the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Vajrapāṇi, entered the samādhi called Vajra-Śrī of the Enjoyment of All Desires; desiring that beloved consort of all the Tathāgatas by means of the wheel of commitment (samayacakra), he became silent.
Then this entire realm of space [was filled] with the semen of the vajra-commitment of the body, speech, and mind of all the Tathāgatas.
[And] it became completely full, remaining like a vase filled with vajra-water;
then, whatever sentient beings in this vajra-space-element were born from the samaya of the three bodies and touched by the glory of the three vajras, they all became Tathāgatas.
The Arhats and Samyaksaṃbuddhas became possessors of the three vajra-knowledges; from that time forth, all sentient beings [became] Samantabhadra.
"Samantabhadra"— thus they were consecrated by the Vajra of the Body, Speech, and Mind of all the Tathāgatas.
Then the Tathāgata Vajrapāṇi spoke thus to those Tathāgatas:

[The Lord of all Tathāgatas: "The Blessed Ones, all the Tathāgatas, have seen the equality of all Buddha-dharmas. Then those all Tathāgatas spoke thus to Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of all Tathāgatas: "We have seen..."

They spoke thus to the Tathāgata: "O Bhagavat, O Sugata, the equality of vajra-gnosis is the practice of vajra-gnosis. Then all the Blessed Tathāgatas, having emerged from the wombs of all the Tathāgata-consorts, [addressed] the Blessed Mahāvajrapāṇi.

The lords of all Tathāgatas spoke thus to the Tathāgata: “It is marvelous, Blessed One! It is marvelous, Sugata! For indeed, it is by means of the syllables and words of passion that the awakening of a Buddha is to be realized.
Then Vajrapāṇi, the lord of all Tathāgatas, said this to those Tathāgatas: “Do not [speak thus], Blessed Ones!”

All Tathāgatas, speak thus! For what reason? Because all phenomena are equal to the space-vajra commitment (*khavajrasamaya*), there is no aggregate of form, no aggregate of feeling, no aggregate of perception, no aggregate of mental formations, and no aggregate of consciousness; there is no element, no sense-field, no passion, no hatred, and no delusion.
"Dharma is not non-dharma.
Then all those Tathāgatas became silent.
Then the Blessed One Vajrapāṇi addressed all those Tathāgatas and Bodhisattvas.

May all the Blessed Tathāgatas consider this secret of the vajra body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas throughout all world-systems. For what reason? Because these Bodhisattvas, Mahāsattvas residing in the ten directions, are indeed worthy of this Dharma discourse.
(From *pdf* 99, p.
148) Then Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of all Tathāgatas, addressed Vajradharma:
"Grasp this, O son of good family, this reality of the samaya of all Tathāgatas; for you..."
He was consecrated by all the Tathāgatas as Dharmeśvara Vajragaja.
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajradharma, having said "So be it," became silent.

Then those Blessed Ones, all the Tathāgatas, caused body, speech, and mind to enter into the syllables of the reality of the three vajras. Then the Tathāgata Vairocana, dwelling within the vajras of the body of the entire triple world, remained silent while focusing upon the equality of the bodies of all the Tathāgatas. Then the Tathāgata Vāgvajra...

Dwelling within the speech-vajras of all the three realms and taking recourse in the equality of the speech of all Tathāgatas, he became silent. Then the Tathāgata Vajrapāṇi, dwelling within the mind-vajras of all the three realms and taking recourse in the equality of the minds of all Tathāgatas, became silent.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.

This concludes the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Vajra Empowerment of the Samaya-Commitment of All Tathāgatas," from the *Śrī Guhyasamāja*, the Great King of Secret Tantras, which is the most secret of secrets regarding the mysteries of the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas.
PDF 99, p. 149) The Eighteenth Chapter.
Now, indeed, the great bodhisattvas, Maitreya and the others...

Having seen, heard, and realized the teaching on the secrets of the body, speech, and mind of the empowerment of all Tathāgatas, according to their true nature, as it is, and in accordance with the samaya, they addressed those Tathāgatas present in that very life:
"Aho! This is the definitive determination of the body, speech, and mind of Samantabhadra!"
They dwell everywhere within the three vajras by means of the triple vajra.

All sentient beings, by virtue of the nature of the vajra of the three times known as "arisen," have attained the state of the vajra of awakening and possess the great supernatural power of the Buddha-vajra.
Oh, how truly marvelous is this! Oh, how peaceful and beyond the senses!
Oh, what supreme nirvana! Oh, what a continuity of saṃsāra!
Then all those Tathāgatas spoke thus to those Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas: "It is even so, O Bodhisattvas; it is even so, O Mahāsattvas."

Then all those bodhisattva mahāsattvas, having gathered together once more and having honored all those tathāgatas with secret and other offerings, prostrated themselves and spoke thus with one voice:
Ah! This means for accomplishing awakening is extremely difficult to find—the tantra known as the Guhyasamāja, the most supreme among all tantras.

We entreat you, O Protector: for the sake of awakening those who are obscured, and out of a desire for the welfare of sentient beings, please explain that which has been spoken by the Speaker of Reality.

Then all those Tathāgatas said this to those Bodhisattvas: "Excellent, excellent, O Mahāsattvas! Excellent, excellent, O mines of virtue! Since you desire to ask about all those most secret points within the Tantra,"
(From PDF 100, p. 150) Then all those great bodhisattvas, their eyes blossoming with intense joy, [k, d: out of joy].
Having prostrated themselves again and again, they ask here about their own doubts.
What is meant by "Secret" here? What is meant by "Assembly"? What kind of connection exists there? And what is meant by "Yoga"?
How many kinds of reality (tattva) have been proclaimed, and likewise how many kinds of the secret (guhya)?
What is meant by the "mystery" (rahasya), and how many kinds of the supreme (parama) would there be?
What is to be known as *bodhicitta*, and likewise what is the *vidyāpuruṣa*? What is to be known as *vajradhṛk*, and likewise what is *jinajik*?
What is meant by "Holder of Jewels" (Ratnadhṛk) there, and likewise what is "Āroli"? What is to be known as "Holder of Wisdom" (Prajñādhṛk), and what is meant here by "Family" (Kula)?
What is called delusion? What is called hatred here? What is called passion? And what is called the thunderbolt here?
Regarding the term *ratī*, how is it said that it is remembered as "attainment" (*sampad*)?
For what purpose is *Yamāntakṛt* [employed], and likewise, what is *Prajñāntakṛt*?
How indeed is one called Padmāntakṛt, and likewise Vighnāntakṛt? What is to be known as Samantacaryā, and what is likewise Mantracaryā?
Regarding the word "japa," what is to be known here, and what is called "sealing"?
How is the *dharmodaya* to be visualized, and likewise, what is *saṃvara* like?
How does one accomplish the welfare of sentient beings through hatred, delusion, and great passion?
What is meant by the "mandala," and how does the placement of the mudrās occur?
(From *pdf* 100, p.
151) Regarding the term "flower," what is to be known here, and what is meant by "caitya"?
How is the wheel of gnosis (*jñānacakra*) to be known, and what is meant here by "state" (*pada*)?
And how, O Lords, does the imperative arise, and how does the incitement come to be?
How is there the vocative for them, and how indeed is there the binding in this context?
How should the consecration be given, and likewise how the vow of knowledge?
How should the five nectars be consumed, and likewise how the five powers?
What is the supreme commonality of accomplishment, and what is it like? How many kinds of means are there therein, and what is the goal like?
How do the yogins issue commands to all the Vajra-holders?
How do they bring about diversity [or the commitment]? Tell me all that quickly.

Then all those Tathāgatas, having heard the words of inquiry from those Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, remained silent for a moment, focusing their attention upon the Great Bodhisattva Mahāvajradhara. Then they—
All the great bodhisattvas, joyful and compassionate in nature,
repeatedly entreat the perfectly awakened ones, the Sugatas, the Protectors.

Then all those Tathāgatas spoke thus to those Bodhisattvas: “O lords of the Bodhisattvas, for the sake of sentient beings, you who possess the vajras of body, speech, and mind, [should act] by means of the vajra of body, speech, and mind.”
Listen to the detailed explanations of the questions.
Then all those great bodhisattvas, having received the words of favor from all those Tathāgatas—
[having heard the words of the supreme secret; having grasped them]— [regarded] the body, speech, and mind-vajra of the Great Bodhisattva Mahāvajradhara.

Having taken as their object the vajras of one’s own body, speech, and mind—[kh, g: with vajra-words they gave the cry of "Excellent!"]—"Excellent, excellent, O Blessed Ones! Excellent, excellent, O Sugatas! [kh, g: O all Tathāgatas! (pdf 101, p. 152).
They became silent.
Then all those Tathāgatas, whose nature is great compassion, took them into their hearts, focused upon them, and empowered them.

With one voice, the great bodhisattvas explained those questions [according to the *kh* manuscript: "all having gathered together with one mind and in one sound"]. Then, having heard the words of the questions from those bodhisattva mahāsattvas, all those Tathāgatas for a moment [addressed] the great bodhisattva...
Having focused upon Vajradhara, he said:
"The threefold body, speech, and mind is designated as 'the secret.
Their assembly is declared to be the 'union' (samāja), which is the designation for all Buddhas."
The fifth, the ninth, the tenth, the seventh, and the thirteenth—
this is the great teaching and practice of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
The fourth, the sixteenth, the eighth, and likewise the twelfth;
these constitute the common duties of the preceptor, as well as the accomplishment and the restraint of the vow.
The eighth and the second, the tenth, the fifth, and the fourteenth.
Forcible attraction, as well as the *upasādhana* and *sādhana*,
the seventh and the third, and the tenth, eleventh, and fifth [are the supreme service and accomplishment].
And for the sake of the field of accomplishment, there is the observance of service and practice,
which is capable of performing the activities of all Tathāgatas— both restraint and grace.
The deliverance of beings who are tamed, wild, or gentle;
the connection with the generation stage; and the vajra-ritual of service—these are the four.
(From PDF 101, p.
153) The ripening of disciples by the gurus through the path of mantra,
for the sake of a great-souled, excellent disciple who has been well-initiated and is firm in his vows.
The teaching and the liberation of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
The meditative union of wisdom and means is designated as "yoga. By their very nature, wisdom is that by which one abides, while means is the characteristic of existence.
The continuum is declared to be the tantra; that continuum is threefold, by way of the divisions of the support, the nature, and the indestructible.

The summary of the meaning of the Tantra consists of three parts: the nature (prakṛti), which is the cause of form; likewise, the fruit that cannot be taken away; and the support along with its means.
The group of five, the three families, and the one hundred and one families of intrinsic nature—
this simultaneous teaching on the Bodhivajra is intended as the *Sottara-tantra*.
Reality is declared to be the five families; the secret is said to be the three families;
the presiding deity is the mystery, and the supreme family is of a hundredfold variety.
Without beginning or end, peaceful, beyond the perception of existence and non-existence, all-pervading,
and inseparable from emptiness and compassion— this is known as bodhicitta.
By means of the vajras of body, speech, and mind, because of their nature of being both penetrable and impenetrable;
when conjoined with the vidyā, he is called the Vidyāpuruṣa.
The five *heti*s and *veti*s are designated as "vajra";
"dhṛk" is known as "retention," and consciousness is the "vajradhṛk-mind."
The middle way is renowned as being neither existent nor non-existent, arising from the primary elements and their derivatives;
it is the body of all sentient beings, the progenitor of the Victors and the Victor himself.

The mind is renowned as a jewel, for it is the source of all objects; that which is certainly to be known by the knower is feeling, and the mind is the bearer of that jewel of feeling. (pdf 102, p. 154)

Through the relationship of the characterized and the characteristic, everything is everywhere and by means of everything; delight is the characteristic, and that which is characterized is called the *āroli*.
That consciousness produced by excellence is called "wisdom" (prajñā); that which sustains the volition of formative forces is described as "the upholder of wisdom" (prajñādhṛk).
The lineage is declared to be the succession; by means of the successions, the origin is spoken of.
That which is indestructible and unarisen is proclaimed as the Name.
Consciousness is declared to be hatred, for it gives rise to or impels the duality of those who hate;
form is known as delusion, by virtue of its nature as an insentient bond.
Feeling (vedanā) is called "striking," by virtue of its nature as ego-grasping (ahaṅkāra);
perception (sañjñā) is essentially characterized by passion and has the defining characteristic of power (śakti).
Conditioned phenomena are always characterized by envy due to their nature of being driven by dependence;
however, the intrinsic nature of the awakened mind arises everywhere within the cycle of existence.
Desire is said to be the mind accompanied by passion, hatred, and delusion;
it is the commitment directed toward that which resembles the universe, the fruit born of karma.
Envy regarding the phenomena of non-dual gnosis is called *ahaṃkāra* (ego);
mutual conflict therein is designated as *dveṣa* (hatred).
The characteristic is passion and attachment; this knowledge is called the Vajra.
Delight is ultimate enjoyment, and prosperity is the supreme bliss of women.
Delusion, hatred, and likewise passion—delight in the vajra is ever-present;
therefore, it is known as the Vajrayāna, the means of the Buddhas.
Phenomena have a nature that is indestructible because their intrinsic being is non-arising;
therefore, the Lord of Death, who brings about the end of all things, is himself the conventional reality of all existents.
Phenomena whose nature is non-consciousness are, from the perspective of ultimate purity, the *samaya* of all minds; therefore, the Victor is the one who brings wisdom to its end.
Phenomena are of an ineffable nature; they are the cognition of non-existence, namelessness, and formlessness.
He is the convention of all phenomena; therefore, the omnipresent Lord is the Destroyer of the Lotus.
All phenomena are non-conceptual by nature, being quiescent in their very essence;
therefore, he is the Lord who brings an end to obstacles, the pledge of all Vajras.
Imperishable, unknowable, inexpressible, and free from conceptual construction—
having realized this gnosis, which is the awakening of the Buddhas, one attains happiness.
Delusion, through the enjoyment of delusion, becomes the exhaustion of delusion and the end-maker of Yama;
by that, one should become the end-maker of the body (the aggregates), and likewise the end-maker of the objects of knowledge.
Faults are exhausted through the experience of those faults; thus, one who brings an end to faults brings an end to wisdom, brings an end to the mind, and likewise brings an end to the afflictions.

Passion, through the enjoyment of passion, becomes the passion of exhaustion; it brings about the end of the lotus, and by that means, it likewise brings about the end of speech and the end of meditative absorption.
That which is the exhaustion of all afflictions is likewise the exhaustion of all karma;
the knowledge that is the exhaustion of all obscurations is known as the "End-maker of Obstacles."
When the pure [mind] is veiled by the vajra of afflictions, all karma is purified;
because all karma is purified, the fruit born of karma is pure.
Grasping, attachment, as well as the immobility of form,
and the states of being cause and effect— through these six, the mind arises.
The six groups beginning with Ṭakkirāja are renowned as the lords of the wrathful ones (krodhendra);
they are celebrated as the elements and their derivatives, and are renowned as the Vidyārājas.
The six beginning with Rūpavajrā are known as the Vajra-lords;
the six beginning with Samayavajrā are the fivefold [deities] within earth and the other elements.
Through the vajras of mind, speech, and body, the Great Beings arise;
their form consists of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, born from wisdom and means.
Having ascertained this through yoga, the mantra-practitioner, by means of the yoga of the completion stage and through the resolute conviction in the purity of all things, being free from all fear,
should move about like a lion with a mind devoid of doubt.
For here there is no such thing as an improper act, nor is there anything that should not be eaten;
there is nothing that should not be spoken, and nothing that should never be thought.
Always concentrated by means of non-concentrated yoga—
whatever practice occurs within all states of mind is called "universal practice" (samantacaryā).
Whatever arises dependently through the sense faculties, objects, and the mind—
that mind is known as "mentation" (manana) in the sense of its being an agent and a protector.
That which is called the observance of the *samaya* is free from worldly conduct;
its preservation by all Vajras is described as the practice of mantra (*mantracaryā*).
Having reflected with the mind upon the respective intrinsic nature of each within the heart,
one should perform the recitation, uttering the mantra according to its divisions as both emanation and reabsorption.

The practitioner of the vow should dissolve the Buddhas, who are of the nature of the universal vajra, by means of the seed-syllable of gnosis; he should meditate upon them as being selfless by means of the seed-syllable of awakening and selflessness.
One should emanate the universe like the universe itself by means of the seed-syllable of the three times;
that is called *japa*, which is declared to be the speaking of all speech as mantra. (pdf 103, p. 157)
That which is proclaimed as "mantra, mantra" is the reality (tattva) and the utterance of the injunction;
it is exactly like the empowerment within the heart and likewise like meditative absorption (samādhi).
Upon their heads there is consecration, as well as worship in every respect;
he who possesses the yoga through the Vidyā is indeed Vajradhara.
Its enjoyments are to be known as fourfold, corresponding to the self-consecration (svādhiṣṭhāna) and the others;
likewise, there is a single sprinkling upon the head for each one of the heroes who possess a single face.
The heart-seal is sealed by means of the mantra-path through the successions of one's own family.
Having sealed the cause with the fruit, and having sealed the fruit with the cause—one must meditate in this way;
otherwise, accomplishment will not arise even in ten million eons.
One should visualize the Vidyāpuruṣa, the wielder of the vajra, endowed with the four enjoyments,
within the three triangles according to the divisions of body, speech, and mind.

One should visualize there, in the center, a ten-spoked wheel that has been turned inward; upon all its spokes, one should contemplate the ten Wrathful Deities, who arise as the nature of the ten types of gnosis.
One should meditate with the completed wheel of cessation, which is supreme and beautiful; one should radiate clouds of vajra-flames that whirl about like something motionless.
Thus, the gnosis of the source of phenomena (dharmodaya) is by nature stainless and auspicious;
through cultivation for even a single moment, the eye of a Buddha arises.
The teaching for the Vajra-holders therein relies upon two stages:
the stage of generation (utpatti-krama) and likewise the stage of completion (utpanna-krama).
The means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), the practice (*pratipatti*), and likewise the commitment and restraint (*samaya-saṃvara*):
all of these are previously explained in detail according to their different sequences.
Sensual desires, such as forms, sounds, and so forth— which consist of pleasure, pain, and both— constantly generate within the heart the arising of passion, hatred, and delusion.
In passion, there is a passion-filled vajra; from the vajra, the Ratnasambhava arises.
Like a jewel, the pledge (samaya) is born; your desires are like the pledge.
Having a form and being formless, all-pervading and consisting of the three syllables,
one should perform the acts of taking up, removing, and expanding through one's own recitation.
In this way, having brought forth hatred and delusion throughout the three worlds,
the Vajradharas perform the purpose that is secret and completely pure by means of the seal.
Having brought forth the circle of hatred through the yoga of hatred for the practitioners, [they act].
Having incinerated [or, according to manuscript *k*: destroyed] with the fierce vajra, one should withdraw [the essence] of the Knowledge-Vajra-holder.
Having expanded those [rays] and awakened them, he should again practice the withdrawal in that same manner;
by practicing yoga thus, he himself shall become Dveṣavajra.
He performs killing and bringing to life throughout the three realms without exception in a mere instant; his power is manifest, there is no doubt.
Having produced the wheel of delusion through the yoga of delusion,
the yogi should always impel all things, such as ornaments and the like.
One should meditate upon the ocean of the deluded mind as being filled with all kinds of jewels;
it shall rain down a shower of gifts for all those who possess the wheel of delusion.
Indeed, with a mind made firm by the Vajra, he performs the giving and taking of all substances without exception in a mere instant.
Having generated the wheel of passion through the yoga of passion, the yogin, having taken it away from all the gods, should desire it by means of the yoga of desire. (pdf 104, p. 159)
Then, with the delights of passion, love, and pleasure, and through the playful transformations of amorous sport,
the holder of the wheel should offer [the oblation] to the five deities.
Even the gods and asuras desire for a moment a wife born within the three realms; how much more so, then, human women?
The mandala, the consecration, the various sequences of ritual actions,
the performance, the empowerment, and the destiny of the perfected ones— otherwise [it would be] different.
The vulva is declared to be the mandala, and the mind of awakening (bodhicitta) is the mandala;
the body is said to be the mandala—thus is the conceptualization of the three mandalas.
Everything is sealed by the seal of the aggregates, sense-bases, and elements;
therefore, one should designate that the mandala is always established by the seal.
One should place the goad, the staff-trident, the form, and the sword in the corners;
and below and above, one should place Ṭakki, Daṇḍabala, Bāla, the wheel, and Sumbha.
The mudrās of the Vidyārājas and other Vajras, as well as those of the six Cakravartins,
and the individual mudrā-maṇḍalas of sentient beings within the elements such as earth and so forth.
A mirror, a lute, a conch, a vessel, and likewise images on cloth—
this is the mudrā known as Dharmodayā, belonging to the Vajra-holders who are the lords of the Vajra.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are sealed by the Wrathful Kings;
other than them, the solitary heroes (ekavīras) are designated according to their family color.
The self-natures (*svadhātu*) of young women are designated as "flowers.
One should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) according to the lineage traditions, through the divisions of body, speech, and mind.
The *caitya* of all Buddhas is said to be the locus of the *ālaya*.
That which is emanated by the *jñānasattva* is known as the *jñānacakra*. (pdf 105, p. 160)
The seed-syllable phrase is proclaimed as the immutable syllable of the three vajras;
it is proclaimed as the impelling and awakening through the nature of body, speech, and mind.
The impelling is the movement of rays throughout the world-systems of the ten directions;
the summoning is the invitation to all those possessing vajras, the invitation to all vajra-holders.
Having withdrawn all vajras into that state by means of the ray of light of all vajras, binding them in the form of a single mass is called the "vajra-binding."
Having sealed body, speech, and mind with the vajras of body, speech, and mind within the mandala of body,
speech, and mind, one should fashion the mandala to be drawn.
In this tantra, initiation is prescribed as having three divisions:
the vase initiation is the first, the secret initiation is the second, and the wisdom-knowledge initiation is the third; the fourth is likewise that very same [initiation].
To the disciple who is a practitioner of mantra, one should give the secret-secret initiation, using a large-eyed woman who is fit for mantra, adorned with flowers, and born of Śukra.
Having placed it in the center of the space-element and combined it with feces, urine, and marrow,
one should assemble all the vajras through the application of the vajra-lotus.
Having caused all of them to descend into the heart by means of the vajras of body, speech, and mind,
one should release them through the vajra-path and cause them to fall into the mouth of the disciple.
This is the supreme state of consecration for all vajras;
all mantras and the extensive arrays of the foremost rites are accomplished thereby.
(From PDF 105, p.
161) One who possesses extreme faith, is highly wise, beautiful, and dear to the practitioner.
The initiate indeed beheld that which was practiced as the single performance of yoga.
The practitioner must indeed offer a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the teacher;
having been requested by the teacher, that [initiation] should then be bestowed upon the practitioner.
O deluded one, through the yoga consisting of delusion and joined with the delight of delusion,
by means of the streams of delusion poured forth, one shall oneself become the Vajra of Delusion.
When one is hateful, through the yoga whose nature is hatred and which is endowed with aversion,
by means of the continuous streams of hatred from the consecration, one becomes Dveṣavajra himself.
In the red [syllable], one should practice the yoga consisting of passion, endowed with the delight of passion;
through the flow of passion from the consecration, one becomes Rāgavajra himself.
The yoga consisting of wisdom-knowledge, endowed with vajra-delight,
becomes wisdom-knowledge itself through the consecration by streams of gnosis.
Having grasped that very deity, the vidyā, for the disciple— the Vajrī—
the hand should be placed in the hand, having made the Tathāgatas witnesses.
Placing his hand upon the head of the disciple, the Guru-Vajrī says:
"Buddhahood is not attained by any other means; therefore, [receive] this supreme vidyā."
All phenomena are non-dual, yet they are characterized by the appearance of duality;
therefore, you should never form an attachment to them within cyclic existence.
This is the unsurpassed vidyā-vow of all the Buddhas;
the fool who transgresses it shall not attain supreme accomplishment.
By its very nature, the five impurities shine forth among the attributes of the body;
through being presided over by the five cognitions, they are known as the five nectars.
(From *pdf* 106, p.
162) Through the application of the mantra-form, one should consume the nectar of the five nectars by means of inflaming, heating, illuminating, and perceiving form.
One should contemplate [the deity] situated in the intermediate space, arisen from the Vajra-hūṃkāra;
below that, in that region, is that which arises in the form of a lotus.
There, one should place the nectar marked with the syllable *Oṃ* in the center of that lotus.
Having ignited and heated it through the union of the vajra and lotus,
the yogi raises up another sun of gnosis, having the appearance of crystal.
Having drawn forth the nectar from the world-systems of the ten directions by means of the supreme weapon, one should consume it by means of the yoga of consumption after having poured it [there].
Likewise, the fivefold hero-substance (*pañcavīrya*) is to be consumed according to the procedure for accomplishing the goal;
having prepared it with the three-syllable seed-mantras, otherwise they do not bestow accomplishment.
The accomplishments such as invisibility and so forth are proclaimed to be "common";
the Buddhas say that the accomplishment which is the means for achieving Buddhahood is the "supreme."
This fourfold method has been described by Bodhivajra;
it is praised— and always proclaimed— by the yogi in all the Yoga Tantras.
The first is the rite of service (sevāvidhāna), the second is the near-attainment (upasādhana),
the third is indeed the attainment (sādhana), and the fourth is the great attainment (mahāsādhana).
Service is of two kinds, distinguished as ordinary and supreme— [according to some versions, it is fourfold]—
the ordinary being by means of the four vajras, and the supreme by means of the nectar of gnosis.
First is the awakening to emptiness; second is the gathering of the seed-syllable;
third is the accomplishment of the image; fourth is the placement of the immutable [syllable].
By means of these four vajras, the common practice and accomplishment are performed;
and in the supreme nectar of gnosis, the practice should be carried out through the six-limbed yoga.
Having performed the supreme practice through the yoga of the six limbs of service, one should accomplish the goal;
otherwise, the highest siddhi will certainly not arise.
Withdrawal of the senses, meditation, breath control,
concentration, recollection, and absorption— this is said to be the six-limbed yoga.
When the ten sense faculties remain established in their own respective functions in every respect,
that is declared to be "pratyāhāra" (withdrawal) for the sake of understanding the nature of nutriment.
In brief, the five sensual pleasures arise from the application of the five Buddhas;
their conceptualization is called "meditation" (dhyāna), and that meditation is fivefold.
Applied thought, sustained thought, joy, as well as bliss,
and one-pointedness of mind— these five are the constituents of meditative absorption.
In all the secret tantras, various types are proclaimed:
the secret, the arising of reasoning (*tarka*), reasoning itself, and analytical investigation through its application.
The third is like joy, the fourth is the gathering of bliss;
one's own mind is to be known as the fifth, which is gnosis capable of the arising of the object of knowledge.
Consisting of all Buddhas, peaceful, and established in all desires;
the breath consists of the five gnoses and has the nature of the five elements.
Having projected it in the form of a single mass, one should visualize it at the tip of the nose as a great jewel of five colors; this is known as *prāṇāyāma*.
Having meditated upon one's own mantra in the heart, one should place it within the *prāṇa* and the *bindu*.
Having restrained the senses and maintaining the jewel, this is known as *dhāraṇā*.
When the mind has entered the vajra of cessation, a sign arises;
that sign is fivefold, as taught by the Vajra of Awakening.
The first has the appearance of a mirage; the second has the appearance of smoke;
the third has the appearance of a firefly; and the fourth blazes like a lamp.
The fifth, however, is constant light, cloudless and resembling the sky;
one should expand that stable [light] through the vajra-path into one's own elements.
Having meditated upon that which is to be recollected, one should clearly recollect its form;
this is to be known as "recollection" (anusmṛti), for a vivid manifestation arises therein.
Having briefly withdrawn all phenomena through the meditative absorption of wisdom and means by means of the yoga of the mass, one should visualize [the deity] within the central image.
The instantaneous accomplishment of gnosis is briefly defined as meditative absorption (*samādhi*);
having attained withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*), one is empowered by all mantras.
Having entered the meditative knowledge (*dhyānajñāna*), one shall attain the state of the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*).
Through breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), one is certainly empowered by the Bodhisattvas;
and through the power of concentration (*dhāraṇā*), Vajrasattva will constantly enter [the practitioner].
From the union of recollection, a circle of light is born.
Merely by mastery over meditative concentration, one becomes free from obscurations;
that mind is to be focused upon in the heart through the application of the four vajras.
Having drawn forth the mind with the supreme weapon and rendered it composed of mantra,
one should recite the verse of awakening through the application of the mantra-form.
(From *pdf* 107, p.
165) Mounted upon one’s own maṇḍala through the meditations on the union with awakening,
that mind, by means of the reflection of gnosis, is the meditation of the *upasādhana*.
As long as vision is twofold, so long must there be cultivation for six months;
one should always and in every way enjoy all objects of desire.
If the vision that was described does not arise even after six months,
one should begin again with three sessions, following the samvara (vows) according to the prescribed rule.
Even when practiced in this way, the vision does not arise for the practitioner;
when enlightenment is not accomplished, one should practice it through haṭhayoga.
Then his accomplishment of knowledge arises through yoga alone;
by means of the application of the divisions of the Kula, one should pin it down with the vajra-wedge.
Then, one should perform the rite of subjugation and protection through the practical application;
having withdrawn the Knower of the Wisdom-wheel (Vajrin) according to the method of great passion.
Having expanded the female consort ninefold, one should place her within the body of the sādhya;
then, having transformed the four mudrās, one should fashion the maṇḍala therein.
Having placed the wielder of all wheels within oneself, one should withdraw them;
having made everything consist of vajras, one should then meditate upon awakening.
When urged in the heart by the four goddesses with songs of exhortation,
one should contemplate the body as the manifestation of gnosis, consisting of the vajra of the three times.
By intoxication the color is divided, and likewise the heart by the flavor;
its own cause is through consecration, and the fruit arises from the division of the support.
By mantra the skin is divided, and even the knowledge-mantra (vidyā) by the Dharma-seal.
Emerging from the *uṣṇīṣa* of the Universal Monarch who possesses the six wheels,
she is renowned as the Queen of Vidyās (*vidyārājñī*), possessing four enjoyments and great supernatural powers (*mahardhika*).
Likewise, those who desire all things should be known as the Vajra Lords.
The consecration of all by means of the meditation-vajra is praised;
through this application of ritual procedure, [one attains] the body together with gnosis.
The means for achieving non-duality through the vajras of body, speech, and mind,
according to the previously stated sequence, belongs to the Vajra-holder, the Knowledge-Person (vidyāpuruṣa).
The creation of the maṇḍala through the self is called the Great Accomplishment (mahāsādhana);
at the time of service, one should rely on the Bimba [deity] through yoga as the Great Uṣṇīṣa.
At the time of the *upasādhana*, the practitioner who knows the ritual procedure should perform the yoga with the deity, whose form is Amṛtakuṇḍalī; during the *sādhana*, he should likewise do so.
And at the time of the great accomplishment, the pervasive Lord Buddha as the image—
this is the supreme secret of all Vajras for the highest yogins.
Thus, by means of this distinction, the Buddhas accomplish supreme siddhi;
otherwise, neither perfect accomplishment nor the highest Śiva arises.
Even in thousands of millions of eons, that which is the union of the goal and the means, even among the Buddhas who are protectors, is called "service."
The union of the vajra and the lotus is called the *upasādhana*;
the *sādhana* is said to be the movement [of breath] accompanied by the syllables *hūṃ* and *phaṭ*.
The nature of space, the mouth of space, peaceful, is called the Great Sadhana;
it is the state of the glorious Lord of all Buddhas, the Great Vajradhara.
She alone is the goal of all Buddhas and the very nature (dharmatā) of all phenomena;
she is attained by yogins by relying upon the garland of yoga in accordance with whatever karma exists within saṃsāra.
Having constructed the maṇḍala there, one should cause [the disciple] to hear the formidable samaya;
first, one should protect the samaya of the Vajra-holder of body, speech, and mind.
Alternatively, by means of those who have arisen through the procedures as prescribed for the *uṣṇīṣa* samaya,
the command of one's own maṇḍala is bestowed according to the specific form of each respective rite.
One should visualize the body of this [practitioner] as the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) by means of the mandala;
furthermore, one should cause him to hear [the teachings] regarding those Wheel-Bearers (*cakrin*) residing within his body.
Then, having caused that [drop] to fall, one should visualize those who have emerged;
drawing them in with one's whole being, one should cause them to enter one's own wheel.
Having fashioned an image of him from the substances as previously described,
one should step upon the linga with the foot, the mind possessed by wrath.
Then, having received the command, one should dispatch the wrathful ones, who are surrounded by various hosts of terrifying beings,
for the purpose of slaying the vajra-holders— the practitioner and the object of practice.
Bound, struck, and enveloped by that King of Wrath, the target—
tormented and overcome with terror— is then drawn forth.
One should cause the image of that practitioner of the three vajras to fall;
one should then stake it with the kīla-mantra at the head, the throat, and likewise the heart.
Having brought down calamities, afflictions, diseases, and those arising from various poisons upon those images, one should likewise firmly nail them down.
Then, by means of all applications— through the possibilities of the prescribed rituals—
one should employ the diagrams, mantras, and other practices according to the specific requirements of the task.
One should perform recitation while treading upon a linga, or perform a fire offering within the mandala of wrath;
or one should visualize oneself being devoured by fierce beings during meditation.

In rites of pacification (*śāntika*), one should have a peaceful mind; in rites of enrichment (*pauṣṭika*), a mind full of nourishment; in rites of subjugation (*vaśya*), having made the mind red (passionate); and in rites of wrath (*krodha*), a wrathful mind. (pdf 109, p. 168) [kh, g: *puṣṭa*; k, kh, g: *krdhān*]
One should subdue the cruel ones. Thus [it is said].

Then the Blessed Ones, all the Tathāgatas, having resolved the doubts of those Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas— acting as the dispellers of all doubts— [beheld] the one who dwells within the vajras of his own body, speech, and mind, the indestructible Body, Speech, and Mind Vajra that cuts through all doubts.
Having taken hold of their own body, speech, and mind, they remained silent.
Then all those Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas praised all those Tathāgatas with this King of Praises:
"Homage to you from all bodies; homage, homage to all speech!"
Homage to you, to all minds; homage again and again to the hearts of sentient beings.

Since the vajras of body, speech, and mind are attained through the state of body, speech, and mind, the Buddhas are equal to the unequaled sentient beings; who then is the object to be accomplished, and who is the practitioner?
If the practitioner, that great-souled one, is not defiled by sins through the obstruction of all Buddhas, then how could he be defiled? And if he were defiled, how could there be any fruit?
Then all those Tathāgatas gave their approval to those great Bodhisattvas:
"Excellent, excellent, O Great Beings! Excellent, excellent, O Great Sages!
Excellent, excellent, O Great Voices! Excellent, excellent, O Great Majesties!"
The glorious master, sovereign of all Buddhas, possesses the vajra of awakening;
he is the agent of the creation and dissolution of all phenomena, which are indeed like an illusion.
For him there would be neither sin nor likewise merit;
for one who has neither merit nor sin, awakening (bodhi) is proclaimed.
Deceiving that Protector is the destruction of all embodied beings;
[for them] an evil rebirth will certainly not arise, and enlightenment will not be difficult to attain.
If, due to a previous terrible deed, one is born in hell,
then for those beings who are hell-beings, there arises a great result.
They become sealed by wisdom; this is the goal of those who possess the vajra of enlightenment.
By that, the supreme benefit for sentient beings is to be known by the yogins.
The activity of subduing and favoring is the duty of the great-souled ones;
having performed the rites up to the great accomplishment (*mahāsādhana*), one should then begin the ritual action.

Then all those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, having heard the dharma of the method of great compassion of all vajras, were pleased, delighted, and thoroughly satisfied, and they gave their approval, saying:
"Excellent, excellent, O Great Protectors! Excellent, excellent, O Great Sage!"
Excellent, excellent, O you of great dharma! Excellent, excellent, O you of great compassion!
Oh, how supremely pure is the compassion of Samantabhadra!
Even for those of wicked intent engaged in cruel deeds, it bestows the fruit of Buddhahood.

Then all those Tathāgatas spoke thus to those Bodhisattvas, Mahāsattvas: "Therefore, noble sons, a mantra-practitioner who has been consecrated in this *Sarvatathāgatābhiṣekaguhyasamāja* must not dwell [in fear], must not tremble, and must not fall into terror. For what reason? Because..."
The great ones, such as Dveṣavajra and the others, who have arisen from the Bodhivajra,
must not be rejected in this continuous compendium of mantras.
Then those bodhisattva mahāsattvas praised all those tathāgatas with a single voice by means of these verses:

That which is the arising of the vajra of the three times, which is both existence and liberation, peaceful, and the cultivation of the pure self-element free from obscuration— that Bodhivajra, the Supreme Lord of the Buddhas beginning with the primordial Buddha— [I worship] with body, mind, and speech.
which is redundant and disturbs the meter; [kh: vajra] we constantly pay homage.

Whatever is form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; the six sense bases and the six faculties; water, fire, wind, earth, and space—we bow constantly to all those vast phenomena that are like the mind of awakening.

We pay homage to those vast states resembling the mind of awakening— those which consist of delusion, hatred, and likewise passion, which are the vajra-phenomena produced through the application of vidyā, which are constant yet false phenomena, and which have become the very essence of a state overwhelmed by various and manifold delights.

We bow to those vast Vajras who are like the Vajra of Awakening: to gathering, to delight, and likewise to the immovable; to the causes, fruits, natures, and the mental states that accord with reality; to wandering, faults, passion, and likewise to obscurations.

We always pay homage to those who meditate upon this pure, beginningless state, constantly engaged in the yoga of wisdom, secret empowerment, vows, and restraints— those who are to be regarded as the very essence of the Vajra of Awakening.
(As stated in PDF 110, p.
171: Those who cultivate this supreme means for accomplishment—the ritual procedure of service (*sevā*) together with the rites of approach (*upasādhana*) and accomplishment (*sādhana*).
We always bow to those supreme masters of practice who are firmly resolved upon the great sādhana, regarding them as the very object of focus, like the Vajra of Awakening.

We always pay homage to those who, like Bodhivajra, are worthy of being observed— those who, through the grace of the Buddha-guru, accomplish various inferior siddhis such as invisibility by means of the four vajras of the twilight periods (*saṃdhyā*) without losing the path, and who are of great renown.
Those who hear this most secret tantra of the assembly, and who recite it, read it, and contemplate it;
those who perform worship, write it down, or cause it to be written—they, like the Vajra of Awakening, are always our object of veneration. We bow to them forever.
And those excellent lords of practitioners who are devoted to this self-recitation, having well-prepared the expansion of rites such as pacification and so forth;
We always pay homage to those who, like the Vajra of Awakening, are marked by the seal of the mantra-known yantra.
Those who teach and touch, who remember and hear even the mere name of the Lord of Accomplishers,
and who place their faith in him and dwell in a single region— those are the Bodhivajras.
We always bow to that which is thus perceived.
With these peaceful verses of praise, one should propitiate all the leaders;
those lords, the Bodhisattvas of great majesty, will then grant their approval.
This well-spoken tantra is supreme, the sovereign of all tantras;
it is the *Guhyasamāja*, the secret arising of all Tathāgatas. Thus [ends here].

When this had been said, all those Tathāgatas and those Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, abiding within the vajras of their own body, speech, and mind, took as their object the body, speech, and mind of the Body-Speech-Mind Vajra with their own body, speech, and mind, and became silent. Thus it is said.

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Empowerment of Vajra-Wisdom through the Instruction on All Secrets," in the *Guhyasamāja*, the Great King of Secret Tantras, the most secret of secrets concerning the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas.
Thus concludes the first half of the body of this king of tantras, the Śrī Guhyasamāja.
